bmt-2020-power-01a.title: Follow the path
bmt-2020-power-01a.body:
The direction is $(0.1,0.3)$, i.e. slope $3$. Moving up from $(0.2,0.6)$ the ball reaches the top edge $y=1$ at $x=0.2+\frac{0.4}{3}=\frac13$. After reflecting its slope is $-3$, so it reaches the bottom edge $y=0$ at $x=\frac13+\frac13=\frac23$. Reflecting again (slope $3$) it reaches $x=1$ exactly when $y=1$, i.e. at the corner $(1,1)$, a pocket.

The trajectory is **degenerate**.

bmt-2020-power-01b.title: Follow the path

bmt-2020-power-02.title: Straight segments cannot return to their start
bmt-2020-power-02.body:
The table is bounded, and a ball moving along a straight line must eventually reach an edge, so a periodic trajectory hits an edge at some times $t_0<t_1<\cdots$ (the set of hit times is periodic with period $C$).

Suppose the combinatorial period were $1$. Then there is exactly one hit per period, so consecutive hits occur at $t_0$ and $t_0+C$. Between them the ball moves in a straight line at unit speed, so the segment from $P(t_0)$ to $P(t_0+C)$ has length $C>0$. But periodicity gives $P(t_0+C)=P(t_0)$, so this segment starts and ends at the same point and has length $0$, a contradiction. Hence the combinatorial period is at least $2$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-03a.title: Compare pocket times
bmt-2020-power-03a.body:
Let $P_1(t+C)=P_2(t)$ for all $t$.

($\Rightarrow$) If $P_1$ is degenerate, $P_1(t_1)$ is a pocket for some $t_1>0$. The ball $P_1$ is still moving at time $C$ (we have $P_1(C)=P_2(0)$, which is a point where $P_2$ starts and is not a pocket), so $t_1>C$. Then $P_2(t_1-C)=P_1(t_1)$ is a pocket with $t_1-C>0$, so $P_2$ is degenerate.

($\Leftarrow$) If $P_2(t_2)$ is a pocket with $t_2>0$, then $P_1(t_2+C)=P_2(t_2)$ is a pocket with $t_2+C>0$, so $P_1$ is degenerate. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-03b.title: Time shifts preserve periods
bmt-2020-power-03b.body:
Let $P_1(t+C)=P_2(t)$ for all $t$, i.e. $P_2(t)=P_1(t+C)$ and $P_1(t)=P_2(t-C)$.

If $P_1(t+T)=P_1(t)$ for all $t$ with $T>0$, then $P_2(t+T)=P_1(t+T+C)=P_1(t+C)=P_2(t)$ for all $t$, so $P_2$ is periodic.

If $P_2(t+T)=P_2(t)$ for all $t$, then $P_1(t+T)=P_2(t+T-C)=P_2(t-C)=P_1(t)$ for all $t$, so $P_1$ is periodic. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-03c.title: Start at an earlier edge hit
bmt-2020-power-03c.body: A periodic trajectory hits an edge (see problem 2), and by periodicity it hits edges at arbitrarily negative times as well. Pick $s>0$ such that $P(-s)$ is a point on an edge, and let $Q(t)=P(t-s)$. This is the trajectory that begins at $P(-s)$ with the same motion, so it is a valid trajectory, $Q(0)=P(-s)$ lies on an edge, and $Q(t+s)=P(t)$ for all $t$, i.e. $Q$ contains $P$ with $C=s>0$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-04a.title: Trace the path
bmt-2020-power-04a.body:
From $(\frac12,0)$ at $45^\circ$ the ball reaches the right edge at $(1,\frac12)$, then the top edge at $(\frac12,1)$, then the left edge at $(0,\frac12)$, then the bottom edge at $(\frac12,0)$ again, moving at $45^\circ$ again. These four edge midpoints form a tilted square, so there are $4$ hits per period.

**Answer: 4**

bmt-2020-power-04b.title: Trace the path
bmt-2020-power-04b.body:
The ball travels along the segment joining the midpoints of two sides (the medial triangle). By the law of reflection it continues from midpoint to midpoint around the medial triangle: base midpoint $\to$ midpoint of the right side $\to$ midpoint of the left side $\to$ base midpoint, with $3$ hits per period.

**Answer: 3**

bmt-2020-power-04c.title: Trace the path
bmt-2020-power-04c.body:
Label the midpoints of the sides $P_0,P_1,\dots,P_4$ counterclockwise starting with the base. The ball goes $P_0\to P_2\to P_4\to P_1\to P_3\to P_0$ (each step skips one side midpoint, which is why the path is a pentagram), and then repeats. That is $5$ hits per period. (This is the case $n=5$, $k=2$ of problem 4(e): the period is $\frac{5}{\gcd(5,2)}=5$.)

**Answer: 5**

bmt-2020-power-04d.title: Tangent-chord angle in the incircle
bmt-2020-power-04d.body:
The incircle of the regular $n$-gon (center $O$) is tangent to each side at its midpoint, so it passes through all $P_i$, and the $P_i$ are equally spaced: the arc from $P_i$ to $P_j$ counterclockwise has central angle $\frac{360\,((j-i)\bmod n)}{n}$ degrees.

The line $C_iC_{i+1}$ is tangent to the incircle at $P_i$, and the ray $P_iC_{i+1}$ points counterclockwise along the tangent. By the tangent-chord theorem, the angle between this tangent ray and the chord $P_iP_j$ equals half the intercepted arc (the arc from $P_i$ counterclockwise to $P_j$). Therefore
$$\angle C_{i+1}P_iP_j=\frac12\cdot\frac{360\,((j-i)\bmod n)}{n}=\frac{180\,((j-i)\bmod n)}n.\ \blacksquare$$

bmt-2020-power-04e.title: The ball visits $P_0,P_k,P_{2k},\dots$
bmt-2020-power-04e.body:
By the fact, $\angle C_1P_0P_k=\frac{180k}{n}^\circ$, so the initial ray from $P_0$ passes through $P_k$ and the first hit is at $P_k$ (a midpoint, not a pocket).

At $P_k$, the incoming ray reversed is $P_kP_0$, and $\angle C_{k}P_kP_0=180^\circ-\angle C_{k+1}P_kP_0=180^\circ-\frac{180(n-k)}n=\frac{180k}n$. By the law of reflection the outgoing ray makes the angle $\frac{180k}n$ with the edge on the other side, i.e. $\angle C_{k+1}P_kP_{j}=\frac{180k}{n}$, which by the fact means $j\equiv k+k=2k\pmod n$. So the ball goes next to $P_{2k}$ and, repeating the argument (the table is symmetric under rotation by $\frac{360}n$), to $P_{3k},P_{4k},\dots$ (indices mod $n$), each time leaving a midpoint at the same angle $\frac{180k}n$ to the edge.

The ball is back at $P_0$ after $c$ hits exactly when $n\mid ck$, and then it leaves $P_0$ at the same angle $\frac{180k}{n}$ as at the start, so the state repeats. The smallest such $c$ is $\frac{n}{\gcd(n,k)}$ (equivalently $\frac{\operatorname{lcm}(n,k)}{k}$). The hit points are distinct before then, so this is the combinatorial period; in particular the trajectory is periodic. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-05a.title: Trace the path
bmt-2020-power-05a.body:
The right side of the triangle has direction $120^\circ$, so a ray at $30^\circ$ is perpendicular to it. The ball hits the right side head-on and retraces its path to the base midpoint, where it reflects off the base and travels at $150^\circ$, which is perpendicular to the left side (direction $60^\circ$); it hits that head-on and returns to the base midpoint, reflecting back to the original direction.

Hits per period: right side, base, left side, base: $4$.

**Answer: 4**

bmt-2020-power-05b.title: Trace the path
bmt-2020-power-05b.body:
The upper right side of the pentagon has direction $144^\circ$, so the ray at $54^\circ$ is perpendicular to it. The ball hits that side head-on and retraces back to the base midpoint, reflects, and by the left-right symmetry of the pentagon goes to the upper left side, again head-on, and returns.

Hits per period: upper right side, base, upper left side, base: $4$.

**Answer: 4**

bmt-2020-power-05c.title: Project $P$ onto the side
bmt-2020-power-05c.body:
Since $n$ is odd, the topmost vertex $A_1$ is opposite the base, and the line $A_1P$ passes through the center $O$ and is a symmetry axis. The circumradius is $R=\frac1{2\sin(\pi/n)}$ and the inradius is $r=\frac1{2\tan(\pi/n)}$, so $A_1P=R+r=\frac{1+\cos(\pi/n)}{2\sin(\pi/n)}$.

The interior angle at $A_1$ is $\pi-\frac{2\pi}n$, and $A_1P$ bisects it, so $\angle PA_1A_2=\frac\pi2-\frac\pi n$, which is acute. Let $Q$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to line $A_1A_2$. Then $Q$ is on the ray $A_1A_2$ with
$$A_1Q=A_1P\cos\left(\tfrac\pi2-\tfrac\pi n\right)=A_1P\sin\tfrac\pi n=\frac{1+\cos(\pi/n)}{2}.$$
This lies strictly between $0$ and $1=A_1A_2$, so $Q$ is on the segment $\overline{A_1A_2}$ and $\angle PQA_1=90^\circ$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-05d.title: Use the symmetry axis
bmt-2020-power-05d.body:
Let $Q$ be the point with $PQ\perp A_1A_2$, and let $Q'$ be its mirror image in the symmetry axis $A_1P$, so $PQ'\perp A_1A_n$. Neither is a pocket ($Q$ is in the interior of the side by the construction).

A ball leaving $P$ toward $Q$ hits $A_1A_2$ perpendicularly and so retraces its path back to $P$. At $P$ it hits the base, whose normal at $P$ is the symmetry axis $A_1P$; reflecting the direction $Q\to P$ in the base gives the direction $P\to Q'$ (the mirror image of the direction $P\to Q$ in the axis). So the ball travels to $Q'$, hits $A_1A_n$ perpendicularly, and returns to $P$, where the same reflection sends it back toward $Q$ with the original direction.

The hits in one period are $Q,P,Q',P$: combinatorial period $4$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-06a.title: Perpendicular bounces
bmt-2020-power-06a.body:
Let $\alpha=18^\circ$, so $\angle C=72^\circ$. The ray from $P$ at angle $\alpha$ with $PC$ meets $BC$ at $D$ with $\angle PDC=180^\circ-18^\circ-72^\circ=90^\circ$, so it hits $BC$ head-on and retraces to $P$. At $P$ it reflects off $AC$ and travels up and to the left at angle $\alpha$ with $PA$; it reaches $AB$ at $E$ with $\angle PEA=72^\circ$. After reflecting off the vertical side $AB$ the ball moves up and to the right at angle $18^\circ$ with the horizontal, and this direction is perpendicular to $BC$ (since $BC$ makes angle $72^\circ$ with the horizontal): it hits $BC$ head-on at $F$, retraces to $E$, then to $P$, where it reflects back onto the original ray.

Hits in order: $D$ (on $BC$), $P$ (on $AC$), $E$ (on $AB$), $F$ (on $BC$), $E$ (on $AB$), $P$ (on $AC$): $6$ per period.

**Answer: 6**

bmt-2020-power-06b.title: Construct the path
bmt-2020-power-06b.body:
Let the right angle be at $A$, with $AC$ the shorter leg (so $AB\ge AC$) and $\alpha=\angle ABC\le45^\circ$, $\angle C=90^\circ-\alpha$. Set $A=(0,0)$, $C=(c,0)$, $B=(0,b)$ with $c\le b$, and let $M=(c/2,0)$ be the midpoint of $AC$.

**The path.** Let $D$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $M$ to $BC$. Since the angles at $B$ and $C$ are acute, $D$ lies strictly inside segment $BC$. The segment $MD$ makes the angle $90^\circ-\angle C=\alpha$ with $MC$. From $M$, shoot toward $D$: the ball hits $BC$ perpendicularly at $D$ and retraces back to $M$. At $M$ it reflects off $AC$ and goes up-left at angle $\alpha$ with $MA$; it reaches $AB$ at $E=(0,\frac c2\tan\alpha)$, which is inside the side because $\frac c2\tan\alpha=\frac{c^2}{2b}<b$. After reflecting off the vertical side $AB$ the ball moves up-right at angle $\alpha$ above the horizontal. Now $BC$ has direction vector $(c,-b)\parallel(\sin\alpha,-\cos\alpha)$, so the direction $(\cos\alpha,\sin\alpha)$ is perpendicular to $BC$: the ball hits $BC$ at the foot $F$ of the perpendicular from $E$. $F$ is inside segment $BC$ because in triangle $EBC$ the angles at $B$ ($=\alpha$) and at $C$ ($<\angle ACB<90^\circ$) are acute. The ball retraces from $F$ to $E$, reflects off $AB$ and travels down-right at angle $\alpha$ back to $M$, where it reflects off $AC$ and goes toward $D$ again, which is the starting state.

**Period.** One period consists of the hits $D,M,E,F,E,M$ (on edges $BC,AC,AB,BC,AB,AC$), none of which is a pocket. The points $D$ and $F$ are different (feet of perpendiculars from the distinct points $M,E$ with $ME\not\perp BC$), so the state does not repeat sooner: the combinatorial period is $6$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-07a.title: Trace the path
bmt-2020-power-07a.body:
Follow the ball (the midpoint trajectory of problem 4(b) has period $3$): from $\left(\frac34,0\right)$ at $60^\circ$ it hits the right side at $\left(\frac78,\frac{\sqrt3}8\right)$, then travels horizontally to the left side at $\left(\frac18,\frac{\sqrt3}8\right)$, then down-right to the base at $\left(\frac14,0\right)$, and reflects at $60^\circ$ again. This is the mirror image of the starting situation (the start was at distance $\frac14$ from the right corner, now it is $\frac14$ from the left corner). The same three bounces in mirror image take it to the right side at $\left(\frac58,\frac{3\sqrt3}8\right)$, the left side at $\left(\frac38,\frac{3\sqrt3}8\right)$ and the base at $\left(\frac34,0\right)$, with the original direction. That is $6$ hits per period (for an odd midpoint period $3$ the off-center trajectory has period $2\cdot3$; see problem 7(c)).

**Answer: 6**

bmt-2020-power-07b.title: Compare with the midpoint trajectory
bmt-2020-power-07b.body:
The ball moves parallel to the midpoint trajectory of problem 4(c), which has period $5$ (odd). Following the argument of 7(c): the distance of the hit point from the clockwise end of its edge alternates between $d$ and $1-d$ from hit to hit. After $5$ hits the ball is on the base again but at distance $1-d\neq d$ from the corner (here $d=\frac35$), so the state has not repeated; after $10$ hits it has.

**Answer: 10**

bmt-2020-power-07c.title: Parallel trajectories hit the same edges
bmt-2020-power-07c.body:
Let $T$ be the trajectory from the midpoint $T_0$ of the base with the same direction. By problem 4 it hits midpoints $T_0,T_1,T_2,\dots$ of edges $E_0,E_1,E_2,\dots$ and is periodic with some combinatorial period $c$.

**Lemma.** Let $\ell=T_iT_{i+1}$. The two edge lines $E_i,E_{i+1}$ are tangent to the incircle at $T_i,T_{i+1}$, so they meet at a point $V$ with $VT_i=VT_{i+1}$: they are symmetric in the perpendicular bisector $m$ of $\ell$. The reflection in $m$ swaps $E_i$ and $E_{i+1}$, and maps the *near end* $N_i$ of $E_i$ (the end of the side containing $V$ relative to $\ell$) to the near end $N_{i+1}$ of $E_{i+1}$, and the far ends likewise. Hence $N_iN_{i+1}\parallel F_iF_{i+1}\parallel\ell$ and $N_iF_iF_{i+1}N_{i+1}$ is an isosceles trapezoid. (If $E_i\parallel E_{i+1}$ the line $\ell$ passes through the center, $V$ is at infinity and the trapezoid is a rectangle.) A segment parallel to $\ell$ from an interior point $X$ of $E_i$ therefore ends at an interior point $Y$ of $E_{i+1}$ with $|N_{i+1}Y|=|N_iX|$ (the trapezoid is symmetric in $m$).

**The parallel trajectory.** Let $P$ start at $p=P_0$ on $E_0$ in the direction of $T$. By induction, if $P$ is at an interior point $P_i$ of $E_i$ moving parallel to the direction of $T$ on $T_iT_{i+1}$, then the segment $P_iP_{i+1}$ ends at an interior point of $E_{i+1}$ (so it is not a pocket), and by the law of reflection the next direction is again parallel to $T_{i+1}T_{i+2}$. So $P$ hits the same edges $E_0,E_1,\dots$ as $T$ in the same order.

**Alternating positions.** Orient the polygon clockwise and let $s_i$ be the distance from $P_i$ to the clockwise end of $E_i$ ($s_i=\frac12$ for $T$). Facing the direction of $\ell$ at departure the clockwise direction of the edge is on the left, and at arrival it is on the right, so the near end of $E_i$ is the clockwise end exactly when the near end of $E_{i+1}$ is the counterclockwise end. Combined with $|N_{i+1}P_{i+1}|=|N_iP_i|$, this gives $s_{i+1}=1-s_i$ for every $i$.

**Periodicity.** If $c$ is even, after $c$ hits $P$ is on $E_0$ with $s_c=s_0$ and the same direction, so it is periodic. If $c$ is odd, then after $c$ hits it is at $s=1-s_0$ on $E_0$, and after $2c$ hits it is at $s_0$ with the same direction. In both cases $P$ is periodic. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-07d.title: Reduce to part (c)
bmt-2020-power-07d.body: Because the trajectory is non-degenerate, run it backward until it reaches an edge at a point $Q$ (it does, since the table is bounded); by problem 3 the rewound trajectory contains the original, so by problem 3(b) it suffices to show it is periodic. Rotate the table about its center by a multiple of $\frac{360}{n}$ degrees so that the edge containing $Q$ becomes the base; a rotation by $\frac{360j}n$ turns a direction of $\frac{180k}n$ into $\frac{180(k-2j)}{n}$, which is again a multiple of $\frac{180}n$, i.e. of the form $\frac{180k'}n$. The trajectory starts at $Q$ on the base and enters the table, so its direction points strictly into the table: $0<\frac{180k'}n<180$ after reducing mod $360$, i.e. $0<k'<n$. By part (c) it is periodic. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-08a.title: Unfold the triangle
bmt-2020-power-08a.body:
Reflect the triangle across each edge the ball hits. The path becomes a straight segment through a tiling of the plane by unit equilateral triangles, ending at a lattice point (a pocket). Put the start at $\left(\frac12,0\right)$; the lattice points are $\left(i+\frac j2,\frac{j\sqrt3}2\right)$. The path ends at $\left(2,\sqrt3\right)$ ($j=2$, $i=1$): the horizontal displacement is $2-\frac12=\frac32$ and the vertical displacement is $\sqrt3=2\cdot\frac{\sqrt3}2$ (two triangle heights). It crosses exactly three grid lines (the three bounces) before reaching that lattice point, matching the figure.

$$\tan\theta=\frac{\sqrt3}{3/2}=\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}.$$

**Answer: $\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{3}$**

bmt-2020-power-08b.title: Unfold across the lower right edge
bmt-2020-power-08b.body:
Label the pentagon $C_0C_1C_2C_3C_4$ counterclockwise from the origin, so the start is $S=\left(\frac12,0\right)$, the ball hits side $C_1C_2$ at a point $X$ and ends at the top vertex $C_3$. Reflect $C_3$ across line $C_1C_2$ to $C_3'$. In the unfolding the path is the straight segment $SC_3'$ and its length equals the length of the real path.

Triangles $SC_1X$ and $C_3'C_2X$ are similar (angles $108^\circ$ at $C_1$ and at $C_2$, and vertical angles at $X$), with ratio $SC_1:C_3'C_2=\frac12:1=1:2$. Hence $C_1X=\frac13$, $SX:XC_3'=1:2$ and the total length is $SX+XC_3'=3\,SX$.

By the law of cosines in triangle $SC_1X$ (angle $108^\circ$ at $C_1$):
$$SX^2=\frac14+\frac19-2\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac13\cos108^\circ=\frac{13}{36}+\frac{\sqrt5-1}{12}=\frac{10+3\sqrt5}{36}.$$
So $SX=\frac16\sqrt{10+3\sqrt5}$ and the total length is $3\,SX=\frac12\sqrt{10+3\sqrt5}$.

**Answer: $\dfrac12\sqrt{10+3\sqrt5}$**

bmt-2020-power-09.title: Count crossings of $e$
bmt-2020-power-09.body:
Let $C$ be the (time) period of $P$. Folding $R$ onto $T$ (identifying $T'$ with $T$ by the reflection in $e$) maps $U(P)$ onto $P$. Each hit of $P$ on an edge $f\ne e$ is a hit of $U(P)$ on the corresponding edge of $R$ (in $T$ or in $T'$); each hit of $P$ on $e$ is a crossing of the deleted edge by $U(P)$, which is not a hit. During one period $C$ of $P$, $U(P)$ therefore makes $k-n$ hits and crosses between $T$ and $T'$ exactly $n$ times.

*$n$ even.* After time $C$ the ball $U(P)$ is back in the same copy ($T$ or $T'$) and, since $P$ returned to its initial state, $U(P)$ returned to its initial state. Any period of $U(P)$ is also a period of $P=\text{fold}(U(P))$, so is a multiple of $C$; hence $C$ is the period of $U(P)$ and the combinatorial period is $k-n$.

*$n$ odd.* After time $C$ the ball is in the other copy, at the mirror image of its initial state; this is a different state (the mirror image of a direction that is not parallel to $e$ is a different direction, and the trajectory is not along $e$), so $C$ is not a period of $U(P)$. After $2C$ the ball has crossed $e$ an even number ($2n$) of times and is in its initial state. As every period of $U(P)$ is a multiple of $C$, the period is $2C$, and the combinatorial period is $2(k-n)$.

Note that $k-n>0$ since two consecutive hits cannot be on the same edge. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-10a.title: One unfolding
bmt-2020-power-10a.body:
Let the triangle have legs $1,1$ meeting at the right angle $C$ and hypotenuse $AB$. Reflect it over $AB$. The image has legs $AC'=BC'=1$ with the right angle at $C'$. The two triangles together have four right angles at $C,A,C',B$ and four equal sides $CA,AC',C'B,BC$, so they form a unit square $CAC'B$, with $AB$ as a diagonal. Deleting the edge $AB$ (the unfolding) leaves the square billiards table: a trajectory in the triangle is the fold of a trajectory in the square.

[Diagram: a unit square with one diagonal drawn; the triangle is one half, the mirror image is the other half.]

bmt-2020-power-10b.title: Rotate around the $36^\circ$ vertex
bmt-2020-power-10b.body:
Let the triangle be $OMW$ with $\angle O=36^\circ$, $\angle M=90^\circ$, $\angle W=54^\circ$. A regular pentagon with center $O$ is cut by the segments from $O$ to the five vertices and to the five side midpoints into $10$ such triangles ($O$ the center, $M$ a midpoint of a side, $W$ a vertex).

To unfold, reflect $OMW$ across the leg $OM$ (giving the isosceles triangle $WOW'$ with apex angle $72^\circ$), then reflect the new triangle across the side through $O$ that was just created, and so on, alternating between the two sides through $O$. Each reflection turns the picture by another $36^\circ$ about $O$; after $10$ copies the angle $10\cdot36^\circ=360^\circ$ is filled and the figure closes up. Deleting all interior edges (all the spokes from $O$) leaves the boundary made of the legs opposite $O$; two adjacent half-sides $MW$ and $MW'$ form a full side, and the result is a regular pentagon.

[Diagram: the pentagon with its five diagonals-from-center and five apothems, one of the ten triangles shaded.]

bmt-2020-power-10c.title: Rotate around a $36^\circ$ vertex
bmt-2020-power-10c.body:
Label the triangle $OIV$ with $\angle O=36^\circ$, $\angle V=36^\circ$, $\angle I=108^\circ$ (so $IO=IV$). Reflect it across the side $OI$ to get $OIV'$: at $I$ the two copies give an angle of $216^\circ$, a reflex vertex. Reflect this union across the side $OV'$, so the two copies meeting along $OV'$ put a $36^\circ+36^\circ=72^\circ$ angle at $V'$: a tip. Continuing to alternate between the two sides through $O$, each reflection rotates by another $36^\circ$ about $O$, and after $10$ triangles ($10\cdot36^\circ=360^\circ$) the figure closes.

Deleting all the interior edges (the spokes from $O$) leaves the boundary $V_1I_1V_2I_2\cdots V_5I_5$: five tips $V_j$ of angle $72^\circ$ (two $36^\circ$ angles) alternating with five vertices $I_j$ of interior angle $216^\circ$ (two $108^\circ$ angles), i.e. exterior angle $144^\circ$. That is the $5$-pointed star.

[Diagram: a star with five tips, split into ten congruent triangles meeting at the center.]

bmt-2020-power-11a.title: Cut a regular $n$-gon into triangles
bmt-2020-power-11a.body:
Join the center $O$ of a regular $n$-gon to its $n$ vertices and to the midpoints of its $n$ sides. This cuts it into $2n$ congruent right triangles $OMW$ ($M$ a midpoint, $W$ a vertex) with $\angle O=\frac{360^\circ}{2n}=\left(\frac{180}n\right)^\circ$, $\angle M=90^\circ$ and $\angle W=90^\circ-\frac{180^\circ}n=\left(\frac{90n-180}{n}\right)^\circ$. So $T$ is congruent to $OMW$; its base is the side $MW$ opposite $O$ (half of a side of the $n$-gon).

Unfold $T$ across its longest leg $OM$, then across the side through $O$ of the new copy, and so on, alternating the two sides through the vertex $O$. Each unfolding rotates by another $\frac{180}{n}$ degrees about $O$, so after $n$ unfoldings we have $n+1$ triangles filling a half-plane angle $180^\circ$: half of the $n$-gon. One more unfolding across the straight edge produced by this (the horizontal diameter) gives the full $n$-gon. Deleting the interior edges, every pair of adjacent bases $MW$, $MW'$ joins into a full side and we obtain the regular $n$-gon. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-11b.title: Use the unfolded polygon
bmt-2020-power-11b.body:
Unfold $T$ into the regular $n$-gon so that the base of $T$ lies on the bottom side of the polygon. Since $n$ is even, the polygon has a top side parallel to the bottom side and directly above it (the polygon is symmetric about the vertical axis through the midpoints of these two sides). A vertical ray from a point of the bottom side (not a corner) therefore hits the interior of the top side at right angles, reflects straight back down, and returns to its starting point and direction: it is periodic with $2$ hits per period in the polygon.

Unfolding a trajectory gives a trajectory, periodic trajectories correspond to periodic trajectories, and the trajectory is non-degenerate (the vertical line meets the top side in its interior and never passes through a corner or through the center, since the start is not the midpoint $M$ of the bottom side, which is a pocket of $T$). Hence the corresponding trajectory in $T$ is periodic. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-11c.title: Count crossings in the unfolded polygon
bmt-2020-power-11c.body:
Unfold $T$ into the regular $n$-gon with center $O$, cut into $2n$ triangles by the $2n$ spokes from $O$ (to the $n$ vertices and the $n$ side midpoints). These spokes lie on $n$ lines through $O$. The trajectory is a vertical line $x=c$ with $0<|c|<\frac12$ (the start is not a pocket) going up from the bottom side.

The vertical line through $O$ is one of the $n$ lines (it contains the midpoints of the top and bottom sides), and $x=c$ is parallel to it. Each of the other $n-1$ lines through $O$ is crossed exactly once by the segment from the bottom side to the top side, and each crossing is a hit on an edge of a triangle (a reflection in $T$). Then the segment hits the top side: one more hit. So going up from the bottom side to the top side the ball hits $n-1+1=n$ edges.

Then it returns along the same vertical line. The polygon is symmetric about the horizontal line through $O$ (a symmetry axis since $n$ is even), and this reflection is one of the reflections used in folding the polygon back onto $T$; it maps the upward path to the downward path in the opposite direction, so the downward path folds onto the same trajectory in $T$ as the upward path (traversed in the same way). Thus the trajectory in $T$ already repeats after one upward pass of $n$ hits. No smaller period is possible: the only symmetry of the polygon mapping the line $x=c$ to itself with $c\neq0$ is this reflection in the horizontal axis, so states of the upward path at different heights are distinct points of $T$.

Hence the combinatorial period is $n$. (Check: $n=4$, the isosceles right triangle: the ball goes base $\to$ hypotenuse $\to$ leg $\to$ hypotenuse $\to$ base, $4$ hits.) $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-12a.title: Unfold into a straight line
bmt-2020-power-12a.body:
Tile the plane with unit squares by repeatedly reflecting the table over its edges. Then the trajectory becomes a straight line $L$ starting at the initial point (we may assume it is on an edge by following the trajectory to its first hit), with direction vector $(\delta_x,\delta_y)$. Non-degenerate means $L$ never passes through a lattice point. The square in position $(i,j)$ (the one with lower left corner $(i,j)$) is a copy of the original reflected $i$ times horizontally and $j$ times vertically, so it is oriented like the original exactly when $i$ and $j$ are both even, and the true direction of the ball in that square is $\left((-1)^{i}\delta_x,(-1)^{j}\delta_y\right)$.

($\Leftarrow$) If the slope is undefined, the ball moves vertically and bounces between top and bottom edges: periodic. If the slope is a rational $\frac ab$ (in lowest terms; $\delta=(b,a)$ up to scale), start at $(x_0,y_0)$; then after moving by $(2b,2a)$ the line is at $(x_0+2b,y_0+2a)$, which is in a square of position with both coordinates even *relative to the starting square* (shifted by an even vector), so it is a point of the same orientation class at the same position in the table, moving in the same direction: the state repeats.

($\Rightarrow$) If the trajectory is periodic with period $C$, the state at time $C$ equals the state at time $0$. In the unfolding this means that $L$ reaches a point $(x_0+u,y_0+v)$ lying in a copy of the table with the same orientation (both shifts even) and at the same relative position, so $(u,v)=(2i,2j)$ with $i,j$ integers. Since $(u,v)$ is parallel to the direction of $L$, either $u=0$ (undefined slope) or the slope $\frac{v}{u}=\frac ji$ is rational. (If the direction has $\delta_x\ne0\ne\delta_y$ then both signs must agree, which forces the even parities used above.) $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-12b.title: Count grid lines crossed
bmt-2020-power-12b.body:
Unfold as in part (a): the trajectory is a straight line with direction $(b,a)$ through the grid of unit squares, and each time it crosses a vertical grid line $x\in\mathbb Z$ or a horizontal grid line $y\in\mathbb Z$ the ball hits an edge in the real table. Non-degenerate means no lattice point is passed, so the crossings are distinct.

The state first repeats when the line has moved by a vector $(2i,2j)$ with $i,j\in\mathbb Z$ parallel to $(b,a)$ (see (a)). Since $\gcd(a,b)=1$, the smallest such positive vector is $(2b,2a)$ (up to sign). Over this displacement the line crosses exactly $2|b|$ vertical grid lines and $2|a|$ horizontal ones, so one period contains $2|b|+2|a|$ hits.

The combinatorial period is $2|a|+2|b|$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-12c.title: Apply part (b)
bmt-2020-power-12c.body:
The fraction $\frac{2020}{2021}$ is in lowest terms (consecutive integers), so the combinatorial period is $2\cdot2020+2\cdot2021=8082$.

**Answer: 8082**

bmt-2020-power-13.title: Horizontal and vertical distances
bmt-2020-power-13.body:
Every edge of the table is horizontal or vertical, so each reflection only flips the sign of one component of the velocity. Hence the speeds in the $x$ and $y$ directions, $u=|\dot x|$ and $v=|\dot y|$, never change, and the slope of the trajectory is $\pm\frac vu$ (undefined if $u=0$, in which case we are done; if $v=0$ the slope is $0=0+0\varphi$).

So assume $u,v>0$ and let the trajectory be periodic with period $C$. Over one period the ball travels total horizontal distance $H=uC$ and vertical distance $V=vC$, so $\frac vu=\frac VH$.

*Computing $H$.* The horizontal motion reverses only at vertical edges, which lie on the lines $x=0$, $x=1$, $x=\varphi$. Rewind to a time when the ball is on a vertical edge (the motion is periodic and the ball must reach vertical edges, since $u>0$ and the table is bounded). Between two consecutive vertical-edge hits the horizontal distance travelled is the distance between two different lines among $x=0,1,\varphi$, i.e. one of $1,\ \varphi-1,\ \varphi$. Over one period, $H$ is a sum of such distances, so $H=\alpha_1+\beta_1\varphi$ with $\alpha_1,\beta_1\in\mathbb Z$ (because $1,\varphi-1,\varphi$ all lie in $\mathbb Z+\mathbb Z\varphi$).

*Computing $V$.* In the same way, the vertical motion reverses only at horizontal edges, which lie on the lines $y=0,1,\varphi$ (the horizontal edges are at heights $0,1$ and $\varphi$), so $V=\alpha_2+\beta_2\varphi$ with $\alpha_2,\beta_2\in\mathbb Z$.

*The quotient.* $H>0$, and $\varphi$ is irrational so $\alpha_1+\beta_1\varphi\neq0$; the number $\frac{\alpha_2+\beta_2\varphi}{\alpha_1+\beta_1\varphi}$ lies in the field $\mathbb Q(\varphi)=\{a+b\varphi: a,b\in\mathbb Q\}$ (use $\varphi^2=\varphi+1$ and multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate $\alpha_1+\beta_1\bar\varphi$ with $\bar\varphi=1-\varphi$; the product $\alpha_1^2+\alpha_1\beta_1-\beta_1^2$ is a nonzero integer). Hence the slope $\pm\frac VH$ is of the form $a+b\varphi$ with $a,b\in\mathbb Q$. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-14.title: The orthic triangle (Fagnano)
bmt-2020-power-14.body:
Let the triangle be $DEF$ (all angles $<90^\circ$), with $X\in EF$, $Y\in FD$, $Z\in DE$.

**A period-$3$ trajectory is an inscribed triangle with the law of reflection.** After a reflection off an edge the ball moves away from the line of that edge, so it cannot hit the same edge twice in a row. With three hits per period, cyclically, the three hit points $X,Y,Z$ are therefore on three different edges: say $X\in EF$, $Y\in FD$, $Z\in DE$, traversed $X\to Y\to Z\to X$ (or the opposite way). The reflection law at $X$ says that the edge line $EF$ is the external bisector of $\angle YXZ$, and likewise $FD$ at $Y$, $DE$ at $Z$.

**It must be the orthic triangle.** Let $I$ be the incenter of $XYZ$ and let its angles be $x,y,z$. Since an internal bisector is perpendicular to the external bisector, $IX\perp EF$, $IY\perp FD$, $IZ\perp DE$. Then $\angle DZI=\angle DYI=90^\circ$, so $D,Z,I,Y$ lie on the circle with diameter $DI$. Hence $\angle ZDI=\angle ZYI=\frac y2$ (inscribed angles on the chord $ZI$).

On the other hand, the angles at $D$: from the law of reflection, $\angle DZY=\angle EZX=90^\circ-\frac z2$ and $\angle DYZ=\angle FYX=90^\circ-\frac y2$ (the equal angles on either side of the edge), so in triangle $DYZ$ we get $\angle D=\frac{y+z}2=90^\circ-\frac x2$; similarly $\angle E=90^\circ-\frac y2$, $\angle F=90^\circ-\frac z2$. The altitude from $D$ makes an angle $90^\circ-\angle E=\frac y2$ with $DE$, and so does the ray $DI$ (as $\angle ZDI=\frac y2$, with $Z$ on $DE$), and both lie inside angle $D$; so $DI$ is the altitude from $D$. Since $IX\perp EF$ as well, $X$ is the foot of the altitude from $D$. Likewise $Y$ and $Z$ are the feet of the altitudes from $E$ and $F$. So the inscribed triangle is the orthic triangle, which is unique; the two directions of traversal give the two trajectories.

**The orthic triangle works.** As $DEF$ is acute the three feet lie in the interiors of the sides (so none is a pocket). Let $X,Y,Z$ be the feet of the altitudes from $D,E,F$. Since $\angle DZF=\angle DXF=90^\circ$, the points $D,Z,X,F$ lie on a circle with diameter $DF$, so $\angle EXZ=\angle ZDF=\angle D$. Since $\angle DYE=\angle DXE=90^\circ$, the points $D,Y,X,E$ lie on a circle with diameter $DE$, so $\angle FXY=\angle YDE=\angle D$. Hence $XZ$ and $XY$ make equal angles with $EF$: the law of reflection holds at $X$, and by symmetry at $Y$ and $Z$. The path $X\to Y\to Z\to X$ is a periodic trajectory with $3$ hits per period (its three hits are on three different edges, so its combinatorial period is $3$), and its time reverse is the other one.

So there are exactly two. $\blacksquare$

bmt-2020-power-15.title: Unfold and shift slightly
bmt-2020-power-15.body:
Let $T$ be the periodic trajectory with odd combinatorial period $p$, with consecutive hits $T_0,T_1,\dots,T_p=T_0$ on edges $e_0,\dots,e_{p-1},e_p=e_0$.

**Unfolding.** Unfold the table along $T$: reflect the table across each edge hit in turn, so that the trajectory becomes a straight line $L$ crossing copies $\Pi_0,\Pi_1,\Pi_2,\dots$ of the table, where $\Pi_{i+1}$ is the reflection of $\Pi_i$ across the copy of $e_i$ it contains. Let $g_i$ be the isometry carrying $\Pi_0$ to $\Pi_i$; it is a product of $i$ reflections. After $p$ reflections ($p$ odd) the copy $\Pi_p$ is a mirror image of $\Pi_0$ with reversed orientation: $g_p$ is an orientation-reversing isometry mapping $T_0$ to $T_p$ (the point of $L$ where $T$ returns to its start), and mapping $L$ onto itself preserving its direction, so $g_p$ is a glide reflection with axis $L$. After $2p$ reflections $g_{2p}=g_p^2$ is a translation along $L$.

**A nearby trajectory.** The line $L$ is cut into $2p$ consecutive segments $Q_iQ_{i+1}$ ($i=0,\dots,2p-1$), each lying in a copy of the table between two edges, with endpoints that are not pockets (the original trajectory is non-degenerate). Apply the theorem to each segment (folded back into the table): there is $\epsilon_i$ such that any parallel shift by $t<\epsilon_i$ stays away from pockets. Let $\epsilon=\min\epsilon_i$ and fix $0<t<\epsilon$. Let $L_t$ be the line parallel to $L$ at distance $t$ (on one chosen side). The trajectory $R$ whose unfolding is $L_t$ crosses the same copies in the same order, hits the same edges $e_0,\dots,e_{p-1},e_0,\dots$ as $T$ and is non-degenerate.

**Period.** The translation $g_{2p}$ maps $L_t$ to itself, so after $2p$ hits $R$ is back in its initial state: $R$ is periodic and its combinatorial period $d$ divides $2p$. Also $g_i$ depends only on the first $i$ edges hit, which for $R$ are the same as for $T$; if the sequence of hit edges has period $m$ then $g_{km}=g_m^{\,k}$.

- *$d$ odd.* Then $d\mid p$ and the edge sequence has period $d$, so $g_p=g_d^{\,p/d}$. Since $R$ returns to its state after $d$ hits, $g_d$ maps $L_t$ to itself reversing orientation, so it is a glide reflection with axis $L_t$, and so is its odd power $g_p$. But $g_p$ is a glide reflection with axis $L\ne L_t$, a contradiction.
- *$d$ even.* Write $d=2d'$ with $d'\mid p$. The edge sequence of $R$ (which equals that of $T$) has periods $2d'$ and $p$, hence period $\gcd(2d',p)=d'$, which is odd. Then $g_p=g_{d'}^{\,p/d'}$ is an odd power of the orientation-reversing isometry $g_{d'}$, and it is a glide reflection with axis $L$; this forces $g_{d'}$ to be a glide reflection with the same axis $L$. So $g_{d'}$ maps $L$ to itself and carries the initial state of $T$ to its state after $d'$ hits: $T$ returns to its initial state after $d'$ hits. As $p$ is the combinatorial period of $T$, $d'=p$ and $d=2p$.

Hence $R$ is periodic with combinatorial period exactly $2p$. $\blacksquare$
